name: Tonnaro
tagline: A specialised-transport marketplace for Georgia — order a crane, tow truck or concrete pump, get a routed, elevation-aware price, and watch it through to delivery.
summary: Tonnaro moves the things ordinary hauliers will not: cranes, lowboy trailers, concrete pumps, oversized loads. We built the platform end to end — a Django/DRF backend with a configurable pricing engine, and three React surfaces on top of it: a public marketing site, a phone-style ordering app for customers, and an operations console for dispatchers. All of it in Georgian, English and Russian.
role: Full-stack. We designed the data model, the pricing engine and the assignment logic, and built the whole front end.

creative.title: Pricing waits for the climb
creative.constraint: The elevation surcharge multiplies the distance line, but a route's ascent arrives from an asynchronous routing call that a customer can outrun by pressing Submit.
creative.detail: The race is closed three times over: the review step refuses to ask for a price while the route is still resolving, every stop is posted with its coordinates as well as its address, and the server re-runs the route itself before pricing whenever a stored summary has a distance but a null ascent. The success test is distance present and ascent not null, because an ascent of zero is a legitimate answer for a flat city hop. A null ascent collapses the multiplier to 1.0 in silence, so the estimate the customer accepts undercuts the price the order is saved at by roughly 7-10% on a hilly route.

creative.title: Zones are a dragged rule chain
creative.constraint: Which rate card applies is not a lookup — a crane hire inside Tbilisi, a run that leaves the city and a 400 km haul are different businesses, and the operator moves the boundaries.
creative.detail: Zone rows are evaluated in the administrator's own drag order and the first active match wins: a keyword zone tests every stop's address, with `within` requiring all stops inside and `crossing` requiring at least one outside, while a distance zone with a null cap is the catch-all. The winning zone then selects a whole rate row out of the type × zone table rather than multiplying anything, so two zones differ in every column instead of by a coefficient. Reordering rows in a table is a pricing change, which is what lets an operator retune the rules without a deploy — and why each keyword list carries the Latin, Georgian and Cyrillic spelling of the same district, since the address text comes back from the geocoder in whichever language the interface was set to.

creative.title: An unpriced offer still holds the truck
creative.constraint: Two dispatchers must not sell the same crane twice, but a job that has only just been offered carries no committed time window yet.
creative.detail: A resource is held from `offer_sent` onward rather than from acceptance, and window overlap is deliberately asymmetric: two open-ended bookings collide, two scheduled windows get an ordinary half-open comparison, and one open against one scheduled does not collide at all. Vehicle status is derived from whether any order is holding the truck and never overwrites an administrator's maintenance or retired. Without the asymmetry a brand-new offer would clash with every scheduled job on that truck and the price could never be sent; without holding at `offer_sent`, one crane gets promised to two customers who are both still deciding.

creative.title: Gradients measured over fifty metres
creative.constraint: OpenRouteService returns elevation sampled from a coarse DEM, so two route points a few metres apart can differ by three or four metres of interpolation noise.
creative.detail: `maxGradientPct` walks forward accumulating horizontal distance until it has at least a 50 m baseline, takes Δelevation over that whole stretch, then advances the start by one point; the profile chart is drawn from a five-point centred moving average rather than raw samples. Adjacent-point arithmetic reports 50% grades on flat motorway, which would print an absurd steepest-climb figure on a quote the customer is about to accept.

creative.title: One restricted stop blocks the job
creative.constraint: Cranes may not set up on central Tbilisi streets during the morning rush and concrete may not be delivered inside the city at night — rules that belong to a transport category, a place name and a time of day, and that can wrap past midnight.
creative.detail: Each window carries a category, a location keyword and a time range, and the check matches that keyword against every address on the order rather than only the pickup — so a single stop in a restricted district is enough to refuse the requested time. A rule spanning 22:00 to 06:00 is held as two ranges, which keeps the comparison a plain containment test instead of a special case. A rule tested only against the pickup is trivially avoided by a job that starts outside the city and ends in the middle of it, which is the exact shape of the delivery the rule exists to stop.

creative.title: One timestamp is the realtime layer
creative.constraint: Both sides of an order need to see the other side's moves on a console nobody is sitting at, with no websocket and no push.
creative.detail: Every write stamps `last_event_at` plus an event type on the order row, and both notification endpoints return the maximum of that column across all of the viewer's orders — not the unread ones, or marking everything read would move the scalar backwards and swallow the next real event. A ten-second poll, gated on document visibility with a single in-flight guard, diffs that one value; a forward move increments a `tick` every page subscribes to, and suppressing the first fetch stops a page load from replaying the backlog as news. Five pages refetch on real activity and stay quiet otherwise, and because audibility is decided by which side originated the event, a dispatcher never hears their own edits.

highlights: Pricing is a configurable engine, not a rate card: zone rules are evaluated in the order the admin dragged them into, and the winning zone selects a whole rate row out of the transport-type × zone table. Per-kg weight, an elevation multiplier on the distance line, a per-day multiplier and a flat floor surcharge compose the total; the company fee and VAT are derived from it rather than added to it. Every one of those is an editable table, with a live quote calculator beside them.

Routes are truck-aware. Every order is costed against an HGV route with a real elevation profile, because a 40-tonne load climbing 2,000 m out of the Mtkvari valley does not cost what the same distance costs on the flat.
Describing the job in free text suggests the right service — 'my car broke down on the highway' proposes the tow truck — from a keyword engine the admin edits per service.
Vehicle and driver assignment is checked, not trusted: licence categories must cover the vehicle, and overlapping bookings are refused rather than double-sold.
The whole product is trilingual down to the content model — every service, category and landing section stores {en, ka, ru}, so an admin edits all three in one form.
The public site is admin-editable: hero, services, stats, SEO tags and the accent colour of the entire application are data, not deploys.
Orders carry their own audit trail — every status transition and every per-field admin edit is recorded and rendered back to both sides.
problem:
Ordering specialised transport in Georgia ran on phone calls. A customer with a stranded excavator or a third-floor concrete pour would ring around operators, describe the job several times, and get quotes that were guesses — because the real cost depends on the vehicle class, the distance, the load, and, in a country that is mostly mountain, how far the truck has to climb.

The operator's side was no better. Which crane is free on Thursday, which driver is licensed for it, and whether the job was already promised to someone else were facts held in a dispatcher's head. Nothing was written down until it had already gone wrong.
approach:
The platform is built around one idea: a quote should be computed, not remembered.

An order captures the job — service, cargo, pickup and destination pinned on a map — and the backend routes it as a heavy goods vehicle, reads the elevation profile off that route, and runs it through a pricing engine the admin configures rather than one we hardcoded. The dispatcher sees a proposed price, a shortlist of vehicles whose drivers actually hold the licence, and a conflict check against everything already booked.

From there it is a state machine with an offer in the middle: the admin prices and sends, the customer accepts, and only then is the resource committed. Every move is recorded, so the question 'who changed this and when' has an answer.

architecture.detail: A phone-shaped React flow — not a responsive desktop form. A multi-step wizard that suggests a service from the free-text description, reshapes its own fields per service, takes pickup and destination as map pins with multi-stop support, and shows the route, the climb and the estimated price before anything is submitted.

The dispatcher's surface: saved-view tabs with live counts, a polled notification bell that only sounds for the other side's actions, per-order assignment with eligibility and conflict checks, and server-side CSV exports that escape formula-leading cells rather than handing a spreadsheet an injection.

Zones, rates per transport type, weight and distance components, elevation buckets, equipment add-ons, company fee and VAT — each an editable table. The same engine serves the customer's live estimate, the admin's quote calculator and the recalculation that fires when a route resolves, so no two screens can disagree about a number.

A server-side OpenRouteService proxy for driving-hgv directions with elevation and steepness, keyed and cached so the API key never reaches the browser and a re-render never costs a request. The client draws the polyline coloured by gradient and a smoothed elevation chart beneath it.

Landing page, site settings, terms and SEO are four singletons with multilingual JSON fields. The colour theme, site name, favicon and contact details are served to the front end at boot, so re-skinning the product is an admin action.

Eleven Django apps, 22 models, DRF generics throughout with explicit per-view permissions, JWT with refresh rotation and blacklisting, UUID-renamed uploads with signal-driven cleanup, and scoped rate limits on every sensitive endpoint.

results: Quoting moved from a phone call to a computed number a customer sees before they commit.
Dispatchers stopped double-booking: the conflict check refuses an overlap instead of surfacing it later.
Adding a service, a zone or a rate became an admin action rather than a deploy.
One platform serves three audiences — public visitors, customers and dispatchers — in three languages, from one content model.
demoNote: The real front end with its Django backend replaced by an in-browser mock: seed data compiled into the bundle, served from memory. Every write works and survives until you reload. Sign in from the banner as a customer or as a dispatcher. Map tiles are the one thing still fetched from the network; routing, geocoding and pricing all run in the tab.

name: Nabadi Barbershop
tagline: A booking platform for a Tbilisi barbershop — pick a barber, a service and a real free slot, and the shop runs its whole day from the console behind it.
summary: A barbershop's entire operation, in Georgian and English. Customers book a specific barber for a specific service and only ever see slots that barber can actually work. Behind it, a staff console runs the shop: the day's chairs, walk-ins, the service catalogue, each barber's hours and time off, promotions, review moderation, analytics, and a permission matrix that decides which of four roles sees what. We built it end to end — Django 5 + DRF on Postgres, and two React 19 front ends on top.
role: Full-stack. The data model, the availability engine and the booking constraints, the permission system, and both front ends.

creative.title: The constraint that quietly locked customers out
creative.constraint: A partial unique index allows one active booking per (customer, service). It keeps arming after the appointment time passes, but a past pending booking appears in neither customer tab — "upcoming" needs start_at > now, "past" needs completed/no_show — so the customer sees nothing and gets a 409 they cannot explain or clear.
creative.detail: An hourly beat sweep (auto_complete_stale_bookings) completes any pending/confirmed booking whose end_at is more than a grace window (default 24h) old, giving staff a full day to mark a genuine no-show first. It is written as one conditional UPDATE, so Postgres re-evaluates the status filter at write time and a no-show committed after the queryset snapshot cannot be overwritten back to completed. Without the sweep a customer is permanently barred from re-booking the one service they had, with no visible cause and no self-service remedy; without the conditional UPDATE the sweep races staff and rewrites their decision.

creative.title: Two constraints, one IntegrityError
creative.constraint: Two different Postgres constraints fire on the same INSERT path: the exclusion constraint (someone took the slot) and the partial unique (you already hold an active booking for this service). Both surface as a bare IntegrityError, and they call for opposite remedies — one is fixed by picking another time, the other never is.
creative.detail: booking_integrity_error_code reads the violated constraint's name out of the Postgres error text and maps it to a distinct API code — slot_taken or duplicate_active_booking — with slot_taken as the fallback for unknown names. The customer app keeps its own fallback that sniffs the constraint name out of a 409 body, for backends that predate the split. The naive single catch tells a blocked customer to "pick another time", which is advice that cannot work; they retry every slot in the calendar and every one of them fails.

creative.title: Reminders keyed on a flag, not a clock
creative.constraint: A reminder dispatcher that looks for bookings near a target time needs a window, and any window silently drops every booking that slid past it while beat or the worker was down. Widening the window instead re-sends.
creative.detail: dispatch_due_reminders makes the reminder_24h_sent_at / reminder_1h_sent_at columns the only source of truth and selects every not-yet-reminded booking whose start is still in the future but inside the lead window, so a missed reminder is caught up on the next beat. A created_at <= start_at - lead clause excludes bookings made inside their own window, because a 24h template that says "tomorrow" must not go to somebody who booked twenty minutes ago. The flag is written only after a successful enqueue. It converts an outage from lost reminders into late ones, and stops the catch-up predicate from texting "see you tomorrow" to a customer already on their way.

creative.title: A password reset that answers nothing
creative.constraint: The endpoint must behave identically whether or not the phone number has an account. Returning 204 either way is not enough: the SMS send only happens when the account exists, so provider latency or a provider outage turns response time and error rate into an account-existence oracle.
creative.detail: The send is handed to Celery rather than performed in the request, and the enqueue is wrapped in a bare except whose only job is to keep the response shape identical — the view returns 204 no matter what happens downstream. The code itself is stored as a SHA-256 digest with a 15-minute TTL and an attempt counter incremented by an atomic F() update; once the counter reaches the cap the row is filtered out of the lookup entirely, so even the correct code is dead. A 6-digit code is brute-forceable inside its own TTL without the cap, and a timing difference of a few hundred milliseconds is enough to enumerate a shop's customer list without ever logging in.

creative.title: One PATCH, five status values, four keys
creative.constraint: Every booking lifecycle action has its own feature flag and its own endpoint, but the admin console also needs a generic PATCH for notes and reschedules. Gating that PATCH as one endpoint gives it one key — and PATCH {status: "completed"} then performs the action whose flag is off.
creative.detail: PATCH is treated as a bundle of per-field mutations rather than an endpoint: partial_update resolves its required keys from the validated body, mapping each requested status value to the same feature key as its dedicated endpoint, and a reschedule that also changes status requires both keys. The viewset deliberately omits partial_update from its action-to-key table so the routing cannot be bypassed by the class-level machinery. It closes a live privilege escalation — an administrator with cancel, complete and no-show all revoked could still perform all three — and a parametrised regression test now asserts the reschedule key alone grants none of them.

creative.title: The API never sends a sentence
creative.constraint: The interface is Georgian-first with English second, and the API is written in English. Any human-readable message the backend returns is a string in the wrong language that a translator can never reach.
creative.detail: Every error response is flattened to {code, message, field} where code is a stable machine token, and both front ends use that token directly as an i18next key — so the Georgian wording of "this slot was just taken" lives in the customer app's locale files, not in Python. The same code also decides the HTTP status through a _STATUS_OVERRIDES table, which is how a serializer raising ValidationError({"start_at": ["slot_taken"]}) becomes a 409 rather than a 400. Content follows the same rule in the schema: name is the Georgian column and name_en is an optional override that degrades to Georgian when blank, rather than to nothing. It keeps the API's error contract translatable and its status codes honest from one table, and means a Georgian customer never sees an untranslated English sentence leak out of a validator.

highlights: Double-booking is refused by the database, not by the application: a Postgres exclusion constraint over (barber, time range) means two requests racing for the same chair cannot both win, however the API is called.

Availability is computed, not stored. A barber's own hours fall back to the shop's, time off is subtracted — a lunch break is entered as one, so there is no second concept to keep in step — the chosen service's duration decides how wide a slot has to be, and lead time trims the front of today, so the calendar only ever offers a slot the shop can honour.

Four roles and one permission table of sixteen keys. Every flag is enforced three times over — a DRF permission class on the endpoint, a React gate on the route, and the sidebar that decides the screen is worth showing. A backend test holds the seeded matrix, the enforcement probes and the key list to each other; the console's own copy of the map is kept in step by a parity checker run over the three.
Every staff mutation writes an audit row with a full before/after diff, including a pre-delete snapshot, so 'who changed this and when' has an answer after the row is gone.
Bilingual to the content model: services, categories and every landing section store Georgian and English side by side, and an admin edits both in one form.
The public site is admin-editable — hero, gallery, opening hours, address, social links and the featured reviews band are data, not a deploy.
564 backend tests and 36 front-end suites holding 180 cases, with the booking constraints and the slot algorithm carrying the heaviest coverage, behind a 78% coverage gate in CI.
problem:
A barbershop's diary is a paper book behind the counter, and it only works while somebody is standing next to it. A customer who wants a particular barber for a beard sculpt at six on Thursday has to call, wait while the page is found, and take the receptionist's word for it. The shop, meanwhile, has no idea what next week looks like until it arrives.

The failure modes are all the same failure: the diary is a single copy in a single place. Two people are promised the same chair. A barber's day off is remembered by one member of staff and not another. A regular's history — what they had last time, which barber, whether they showed up — exists only in somebody's memory.
approach:
The booking rules belong in the system that holds the bookings, so that is where we put them.

A slot is offered only if the barber works then, is not on time off, is not already booked, and the service fits before closing. That single question is answered by one availability engine, and the customer's calendar, the reception desk's walk-in screen and the admin's day view all ask it — so no two screens can disagree about whether a chair is free. Underneath, a Postgres exclusion constraint makes the overlap physically impossible rather than merely unlikely.

Around that sits the rest of a shop: a service catalogue with per-barber price and duration overrides, working hours that fall back to the shop's, time off that can be one barber's or everyone's, promo codes with use limits, reviews a customer can only leave for an appointment they actually attended, and an audit trail over all of it.

architecture.detail: A four-step booking wizard — service, barber, day, time — that keeps its state in Zustand so a refresh or a back button does not lose the booking half-made. The landing page, gallery, opening hours and contact details are served from the CMS, so the shop edits its own front page.

The shop's working surface: a day calendar with a lane per barber, the booking list with its filters and its XLSX export, walk-in entry at the desk, customer histories with private staff notes, review moderation, analytics, and the permission matrix itself.

One module answers 'when can this barber do this service'. Per-barber working hours with a shop-hours fallback, barber-specific and shop-wide time off (which is also how a lunch break is entered), service duration and per-barber overrides, minimum lead time and maximum booking horizon — all resolved in Asia/Tbilisi, which is the only timezone the shop has ever cared about.

Four roles — admin, administrator, barber, customer — over a seeded feature-flag table. The backend enforces it with a DRF permission class, the console gates the route and hides the nav entry, and a parity checker is run over the three to keep them in step, because a permission that is enforced in two places out of three is a bug waiting for a deep link.

Eleven Django apps, 19 models, DRF with explicit per-view permissions, JWT in HttpOnly cookies with rotation and blacklisting, a single error envelope every endpoint speaks, and Celery for the reminder SMS and the sweep that closes yesterday's unfinished appointments.

Landing content and site settings are singletons with paired Georgian/English columns; booking policy — slot granularity, lead time, how far ahead you may book, the cancellation window — is configuration the admin edits, not constants we compiled in.

results: The chair a customer is offered is one the shop can actually honour — the constraint that prevents a double booking lives in the database, so no code path can get around it.
The shop's diary stopped being a single copy in a single place: the desk, the barber and the customer all read the same day.
Opening hours, prices, services, promotions and the whole front page became admin actions rather than deploys.
Every staff change to a booking, a customer or a price is recoverable from an audit row, including the ones that deleted something.
demoNote: Both front ends, with the Django backend replaced by an in-browser mock: seed data compiled into the bundle, served from memory. The two apps ship as one bundle over one store, so a booking you make on the site is waiting in the console when you switch — the banner in the corner signs you in as a customer or as staff. No seeded row is ever written to storage, so a reload restores the pristine shop.

name: Printomato
tagline: A fleet console for photo-printing kiosks — live device presence, paper levels, campaigns and card payments on one screen.
summary: Printomato runs photo-printing kiosks in malls, festivals and hotel lobbies. We built the operator side of it: a session-authenticated REST API next to the existing device API, and a React console that shows the whole fleet in real time — who is online, who is out of paper, what printed today, and which payments settled.
role: Full-stack, on a two-developer project. We owned the payment stack, the admin API, the React console and the containerised deploy.

creative.title: Cookie socket refuses cross-site openers
creative.constraint: `ALLOWED_HOSTS = ['*']` makes Channels' `AllowedHostsOriginValidator` a no-op, and the fleet socket is the first WebSocket in the project authenticated by session cookie rather than by device id.
creative.detail: `FleetConsumer` compares the `Origin` header's netloc against `Host` itself, closing 4403 on a mismatch and 4401 when anonymous, while an absent `Origin` is allowed because that means a non-browser client (the kiosks). The console's backoff then refuses to retry those two codes, and the demo nginx forwards `$http_host` — port included — plus `Origin`, so the comparison survives the proxy. Without it any page a signed-in operator visited could open `/ws/fleet/` with their cookie and read the whole fleet; without the client half, a permanent refusal would be retried forever.

creative.title: Two aggregates, not one
creative.constraint: The dashboard wants fleet paper totals and photo counts in the same payload, but one `aggregate()` over Device joins Photo, so each device's `paper_count` is summed once per photo it has printed.
creative.detail: `dashboard_analytics()` deliberately runs device scalars, photo counts and payment revenue as three separate `aggregate()` calls and merges the dicts, with the reason written above the code and a regression test that inserts prints and asserts the paper total is unchanged. The single-query version inflated the fleet's remaining paper roughly twelvefold — the number an operator reads to decide whether to drive to a mall with a box of paper.

creative.title: One overlay stack for four layers
creative.constraint: The modal, the photo lightbox, the command palette and the mobile drawer can nest, and each had hand-rolled its own body-scroll lock and Escape handler.
creative.detail: `useOverlay` keeps a module-level refcount and a stack of symbols: only the outermost layer restores `body.style.overflow` and the scrollbar-width padding it added, only the topmost acts on Escape, Tab is trapped inside the container, and focus returns to whatever opened the layer, preferring a `[data-autofocus]` target. The previous per-component version left the page permanently unscrollable after deleting a photo from inside the lightbox, and a single Escape collapsed every open layer at once.

creative.title: The QR token's authority lives elsewhere
creative.constraint: A QR code on a kiosk screen can be photographed, and the payment service that serves it is public.
creative.detail: The QR carries `device_id` plus a token; `/pay` resolves the device through Printomato's own device API and compares the supplied token with the value stored there, then mints `secrets.token_urlsafe(32)` and pushes it back over the shared-secret endpoint before rendering the page. The payment service keeps no token table — an earlier commit removed it — so `Device.payment_token` is the only copy, and `_extract_device_token` walks four candidate field names so a rename upstream degrades to a validation error rather than an accepted blank. A photographed QR would otherwise stay payable indefinitely, and two copies of the token in two databases would eventually disagree about which one is current.

creative.title: RSA padding as a runtime setting
creative.constraint: The provider's reference snippet ships a `use_pkc_padding` boolean, its documentation specifies OAEP with a SHA-256 digest and SHA-1 MGF1, and the live deployment ran PKCS#1 v1.5 — three answers to one question, on a channel where the wrong guess yields opaque ciphertext rather than an error.
creative.detail: `KEEPZ_RSA_PADDING_MODE` selects among `PKCS1V15`, `OAEP_SHA256_SHA1` and `OAEP_SHA256_SHA256` through a single `_rsa_padding()` that both the AES key wrap and the unwrap read, an unrecognised value raises instead of quietly defaulting, and both directions re-raise as a message naming the setting to check. Hardcoding the documented scheme produces undecryptable payloads with nothing to indicate which end is wrong; here a tenant on a different scheme is an environment variable, not a deploy.

creative.title: A command cannot rewrite its envelope
creative.constraint: `Device.give_command` builds the channel message and then does `message.update(payload)`, while the admin endpoint lets an operator attach an arbitrary payload to a command.
creative.detail: The viewset strips `type`, `command` and `message` from the submitted payload before handing it over, and reports delivery honestly: `delivered` is `device.is_online`, because the channel layer accepting a message says nothing about a kiosk consuming it, and a channel-layer failure returns 502 naming the undelivered command rather than a cheerful 200. A caller-supplied `type` would route the event to a different consumer handler entirely, and a "sent" reply for a command nobody received is worse than an error.

highlights: Kiosks hold a WebSocket open — connecting flips a device online and broadcasts presence to every console watching, so the fleet grid never needs a refresh button.
Twenty-seven session-authenticated routes were added alongside the device API rather than on top of it: the kiosks and the original server-rendered pages kept working untouched throughout.

Paper percentage, prints today, campaign progress and open-alert state are all computed server-side — the percentages in the serializer, the counts as queryset annotations — so no two screens can disagree about the same number.
KEEPZ card payments: a shared-secret endpoint mints a per-device token, triggers the flow on the kiosk over its socket, and logs every session as it settles.
96 Django tests, 73 of them pinning the admin API's contract — filters, pagination edges, validation messages, permissions.
One `docker compose up` brings the whole stack — Postgres, Redis, Daphne, nginx — to a seeded, sign-in-able console.
problem:
Printomato runs photo-printing kiosks — mall atriums, festival stands, hotel lobbies. Each kiosk prints branded photos for whichever campaign is live at that venue, and each one eventually runs out of paper, loses sight of its camera, or drops off the network at the worst possible moment.

Operations ran on server-rendered Django pages: one for campaigns, one for devices, one for photos. They worked, but they only ever showed what was true the last time somebody pressed refresh. Answering which kiosks are down right now meant reloading four tabs and trusting the oldest one. Then the kiosks started taking card payments, which added a second live thing to watch and nowhere good to watch it from.
approach:
The rewrite was scoped to the operator, not to the fleet. The kiosks were left completely alone — they still POST to the same photo endpoint, still open the same WebSocket, still call the payment endpoints with the same shared secret. A second, session-authenticated API went in beside the first at `/api/admin/`, and a React single-page console mounted at `/app/` to consume it. The old server-rendered pages stayed live on their original URLs the whole time, so there was never a cutover weekend to survive.

Anything an operator has to trust is computed server-side from a single annotated queryset — paper percentage, prints today, campaign progress, whether a device has open alerts — never reassembled in the browser. On the client, every endpoint gets exactly one TanStack Query hook, and that hook file is also where cache keys and invalidation live. Editing a device refreshes the fleet grid and the dashboard because that rule is written down once instead of repeated across eight components.

architecture.detail: Each device holds a WebSocket open on its own channel. Connecting marks it online and broadcasts presence to the fleet group; dropping the socket clears it. Commands — reprint, reboot, start a payment — travel back down the same connection.

One ASGI application serves the REST surface and three channel routes: the per-device socket, a fleet channel the console subscribes to, and a notifications channel that drives alert toasts. Redis is the channel layer. The containerised console runs a single Daphne for both HTTP and WebSockets; the original compose keeps gunicorn on the WSGI app beside a separate Daphne for /ws/.

Five domain models — Campaign, Device, Photo, Notification, PaymentSession — beside a custom user. Manager methods annotate online-device counts, print totals and campaign state onto the queryset, so a list view does not fan out into a query per kiosk.

Twenty-seven session-authenticated routes under `/api/admin/`: five viewsets plus auth, dashboard and options endpoints, with query filtering, a page-size-capped pagination envelope and an OpenAPI schema generated by drf-spectacular.

React 18 in strict TypeScript, Vite 6, Tailwind v4 with a CSS-first theme block and no config file, TanStack Query v5 for server state, React Router v6 under a `/app` basename. Eleven route paths, code-split past the dashboard, 113 KB gzipped on first load.

The public payment service authenticates with a shared-secret header to store a per-device token, trigger the flow on a kiosk and upsert the resulting session record. The console reads that ledger back with a summary computed over whatever filters are applied — revenue, success rate, rejections.

Pillow generates a thumbnail on save. Files land on local disk in development and in an S3-compatible bucket in production, behind the same storage interface. Bulk-selected photos stream back as a single ZIP.

A dedicated compose file builds the console in a Node stage, collects static in the Python stage and puts nginx in front, then migrates, seeds and serves — one command from clone to a console you can sign in to.

results: Fleet state is live. A kiosk losing its connection greys out on every open console immediately, and comes back the same way, with nobody pressing refresh.
One place to look. Paper, prints, campaigns, alerts and payment sessions share a dashboard instead of four browser tabs of varying age.
Nothing on the floor had to change. The device API and the original server-rendered pages both kept working through the entire rewrite — the new console was additive, not a migration.
The API's behaviour is pinned by 73 tests of its own: filter semantics, the pagination envelope, the exact validation messages the forms render inline, and who is allowed to call what.

The status palette was validated with a colour checker rather than chosen by eye — it clears WCAG AA on the panel surface and holds a wide separation under deuteranopia, and every status ships an icon and a text label so colour is never the only signal.
The whole stack starts from a single command, which is the reason a clickable demo of it exists at all.
demoNote: The demo runs the real console front-end: the same React components, the same TanStack Query cache, the same stylesheet that ships against Django. What it does not run is Django. Underneath, the fetch layer is swapped for an in-browser mock that serves seeded data and applies your writes to an in-memory store — no server, no database, no backend of any kind. There is no third-party request at all — the fonts ship in the bundle with everything else. Every screen is interactive and every edit sticks for the session; reload and you get a pristine dataset back. Fleet telemetry is simulated on a timer instead of arriving over a socket, so devices really do drop offline and prints really do land while you watch.

name: Gisheri
tagline: A natural-stone jewellery shop in Tbilisi — browse by zodiac sign, take the quiz, check out with a discount code, and run the whole catalogue and order book from the console behind it.
summary: Gisheri sells handmade stone bracelets and pendants, and the whole product is bilingual down to the content model: every product, collection and zodiac sign stores its Georgian text beside its English, and Georgian is the default. We built it end to end — a Django 5 + Ninja API with JWT auth, an audit trail and a role-gated admin surface, and a React 19 storefront and console on top of it.
role: Full-stack. We designed the data model, the discount and order pipeline and the two-layer catalogue i18n, and built the whole front end.

items: JSONField for tag arrays and quiz banks

creative.title: The client never names a price
creative.constraint: Checkout is a public endpoint, and the cart already knows the subtotal, the discount and the total — the browser is holding every number the order needs.
creative.detail: `OrderCreateIn` carries no money at all: line items are `product_id` / `size` / `quantity`, and the discount is a bare code string. The server re-reads each product, computes line totals and the subtotal in `Decimal`, resolves the code itself, and only then writes the row. Every figure on the order is one the server derived. A posted total is a price the customer chose. Without this the cheapest attack on the shop is a curl command, and the snapshot columns would faithfully record the wrong amount forever.

creative.title: A usage cap kept by an absence
creative.constraint: The discount admin needs to see how many times a code has been redeemed, and the same endpoint writes every other field on that code with a blind `setattr` sweep over the whole payload.
creative.detail: `uses_count` is declared on `DiscountOut` and deliberately not on `DiscountIn`. The counter is therefore unreachable from the admin PATCH — not by a guard that could be forgotten, but because the field does not exist on the write shape. Its only writer is `create_order_for_user`, which increments it inside the same `transaction.atomic` block that took `select_for_update()` on the row. One shared schema, the obvious move, would let an admin editing an expiry silently reset a redemption count — and would leave the max-uses cap enforceable only by whoever remembered to exclude the field.

creative.title: One predicate, one skip flag
creative.constraint: The shop's six purposes, twelve signs and three genders all show counts, and each count has to answer "how many if I add this" against whatever filters are already on.
creative.detail: A single `matches(product, opts)` takes a set of `skip*` flags naming the dimension to ignore. Each facet counts with every other filter live and its own dimension switched off, so the numbers change as you filter and a zero means the option is genuinely dead. `unisex` counts into both gendered facets, matching how the filter itself behaves. Counting the filtered result set instead — the default reflex — makes every facet in a group show the same number, and picking a zero-count option is the only way to discover it was empty.

creative.title: Language is one attribute
creative.constraint: Georgian is the default language and Playfair Display carries no Georgian glyphs, so the shop's display face simply does not exist in the language most of its customers read.
creative.detail: An `i18n.on("languageChanged")` handler writes `document.documentElement.lang`, and `[lang="ka"]` rules in `index.css` swap both families — Noto Sans Georgian for body, Noto Serif Georgian for headings, so the serif/sans hierarchy survives the switch. The same value drives `og:locale` and `og:locale:alternate`, and is the `lang` a screen reader announces. Set the font per component and the Georgian storefront quietly renders in whatever the OS picks, with headings and body indistinguishable; forget the attribute and the page claims to be in the wrong language to crawlers and assistive tech alike.

creative.title: One refresh in flight
creative.constraint: Access tokens last thirty minutes and the admin dashboard opens with several parallel queries. When the token has just expired, all of them get a 401 in the same tick.
creative.detail: `tryRefresh` stores its own promise in a module-level `refreshPromise` and hands that same promise to every later caller until it settles, clearing it in a `finally`. The first 401 refreshes; the rest wait on it and retry with the token it produced. Without the latch a single expiry fans out into one refresh POST per in-flight request, each racing to write `localStorage`, and the last writer wins — a class of bug that only appears on a page that loads more than one thing at once.

creative.title: A phone order mints a claimable account
creative.constraint: Staff take orders over the phone from customers who have never registered, but `Order.user` is a non-null foreign key and the customer history pages aggregate per user.
creative.detail: `admin_create_order` matches the customer case-insensitively by email and, failing that, creates a `customer`-role user with `set_unusable_password()` and the name split off the shipping field. The order gets a real owner, the spend rollup starts from the first phone call, and the person can later adopt the account through the ordinary password-reset flow. `on_delete=PROTECT` on `Order.user` and `OrderItem.product` then means nothing with a sales history can be deleted out from under it. A nullable user or a free-text name splits the same customer across the web and the phone, and no amount of later reconciliation puts a returning regular's history back together.

highlights: Georgian is the default language, and the catalogue resolves it in two layers: a database column per translated field for anything an admin writes, and an i18n key for the content that shipped with the app, with canonical English as the floor.
The admin console is a full second surface inside the same SPA — eighteen pages, role-gated at the route and again at the API, sharing one sortable table, one date-range hook and one activity feed.

Discounts are re-validated atomically at order creation, not just at the cart: a code that passed the check can still be refused a second later, and the order create path is the only thing that moves the usage counter.

Order lines are snapshots — name, image and unit price are frozen at the moment of sale, so a later price edit never rewrites history, and the admin item editor recomputes the totals without re-evaluating the discount.

Every admin change to an order — and every role or activation change to a customer — writes an audit row, and both of those pages render their own feed from it: who changed what, when, and from what to what.
The quiz scores the live catalogue against a zodiac sign, a mood and an intention rather than a curated answer key, and all four question banks are admin-editable.
SEO is data: a settings singleton supplies the defaults and a per-path override table beats them, both edited from the console rather than deployed.
problem:
A jewellery workshop making stone bracelets by hand had a catalogue that lived in a spreadsheet and an order book that lived in a phone. New designs were announced on Instagram, prices were typed back at customers from memory, and how many of a piece were left was whatever the person answering the phone remembered. Nothing recorded what a returning customer had bought before, so the shop met every regular as a stranger.

The shop's customers do not shop by product name either. They arrive asking what suits a Scorpio, or for something to calm a friend who is anxious, or for a gift that carries a meaning — questions a list of names and prices cannot answer. They also arrive reading Georgian, and every piece therefore has to be described twice, in both languages, by the person who made it, before it can be sold to either kind of visitor.
approach:
The catalogue is the product, so the catalogue is what the admin owns outright. A piece carries its stones, its purposes, its zodiac signs and its price, and every screen that sells it — the shop's facets, the collection pages, the twelve zodiac pages, the quiz — is a query over those fields rather than a list somebody curated by hand. Adding a stone to a sign, or a bracelet to a collection, is a form in the console, and for collections, zodiac pages, the quiz and site settings the storefront's cache is invalidated in the same session, so the change is visible without a deploy.

Every translated field is a column pair, not a translation file. A product stores its Georgian name beside its English one, because a translation the shop has to write is data and belongs where the data is; only the fixed UI chrome stays in i18next. The resolver is one documented order — the Georgian column, then the i18n key for seeded content, then canonical English as the floor — so a piece nobody has finished translating degrades into something readable rather than a blank.

The order pipeline is deliberately small: no shipping calculator, no tax engine, one discount code. What it does do carefully is the part that costs money when it is wrong. The code is re-validated at order creation under a row lock instead of being trusted from the cart, so a code that was live a second ago can still be refused and the usage cap cannot be raced; every line snapshots the name, image and price it sold at; and every admin hand that touches an order or a customer leaves an audit row behind it.

architecture.detail: React 19 with TanStack Query over the four catalogue reads and plain component state everywhere the state is genuinely local. The shop's filters — purpose, sign, gender, price, sort, page — live in the URL, so a filtered view is a link, and every facet count is computed against the live set so a dead filter is visibly dead.

Eighteen lazy-loaded pages behind one role gate, sharing a single sortable, paginated table, one date-range hook and one activity feed. It is a second surface inside the same bundle as the shop, so an order placed at checkout is in the order book on the next read.

Two layers and a documented resolution order: the translated database column, the i18n key, then canonical English. The active language is read off the i18next instance rather than threaded through props, so a component rendering a product name needs to know nothing about any of it.

One create path serves customer checkout and staff phone orders. It re-validates the code under `SELECT FOR UPDATE` and enforces the usage cap there rather than at the cart, snapshots every line at the price it sold for, and lets the admin item editor recompute the totals without re-evaluating the discount — so an amended order keeps the deal it was given.

A settings singleton holds the hero copy, the banner, the featured collections and the SEO defaults, and a per-path override table beats it. Both are edited from the console, so the front page and the meta tags are data rather than a deploy.

Seven Django apps and 12 models on Postgres, with django-ninja routers mounted twice — a public router and an admin router per app — JWT from django-ninja-jwt, camelCase on the wire, and money serialised as decimal strings, so no price passes through a float anywhere on the server or the wire.
Docker Compose: Postgres, Django, Vite, with the migrations committed. One command from a clone to a seeded shop you can sign in to.

results: The catalogue moved out of a spreadsheet: adding a product, a collection or a zodiac description became an admin action rather than a deploy.
Georgian stopped being an afterthought — the shop reads natively in its own market and falls back to English only where nobody has written the Georgian yet.
Phone orders and web orders became the same object, with the same discount rules, the same snapshots and the same audit trail.
A discount code cannot be over-redeemed by two people checking out at once, because the cap is enforced where the order is written rather than where the code is offered.
Staff can see, for any customer, what they have spent and when they last ordered, without leaving the order in front of them.
demoNote: The real front end with its Django backend replaced by an in-browser mock: seed data compiled into the bundle, served out of memory behind the same latency and the same error bodies the API would have returned. Every write works — place an order as a customer and it is waiting in the console, audit trail and all — and nothing is persisted, so a reload restores the pristine shop. The banner in the corner signs you in as a customer or as an administrator, through the real login form rather than around it. Unlike the shop it is ported from, the demo opens in English; the switch in the header puts the whole thing, console included, back into Georgian. There is no network request of any kind — no API, no fonts, no analytics — so it runs offline and in an iframe.

name: Tova
tagline: A lead-capture arcade game for trade fairs — visitors catch falling sponsor coins for sixty seconds, answer trivia and climb a live board, while organisers run the event and export every lead from a console.
summary: A stand at a trade fair has one problem: nobody wants to hand over their details for nothing. Tova gives them a reason. A visitor registers, plays a sixty-second canvas round catching sponsor coins and dodging hazards, answers timed trivia for bonus points and watches a live standings board. Behind it, an organiser console runs the whole event: the schedule, the fairness caps, the falling items, the trivia, the prizes, the people, and the lead list as an Excel file ready for a CRM. Four roles see four different slices of it, in Georgian and English. We built it end to end — a Next.js app, a hand-written canvas engine and the route handlers behind both.
role: Full-stack. The game engine and its fairness plan, the scoring and standings rules, the organiser console, the data model, sign-in, and the bilingual interface.

items: Noto Sans and Noto Serif Georgian
zod validation on every route handler
Signed JWT sessions in an httpOnly cookie

creative.title: A round that is fair before the first coin falls
creative.constraint: Two visitors at a stand compete for the same prize, so luck in the spawns cannot decide it — yet a game where everything is identical is not a game. Rolling a random spawn each frame hands one player a rich run and another a poor one.
creative.detail: `buildPlan` lays out the whole round up front. Every player gets exactly the event's catchable budget and exactly its penalty budget, on a four-stage ramp, with spawn times arranged so each item can still reach the paddle before the round ends. Only the arrangement is random. The server clamps a submitted score to `[-maxBad, maxGood]` as well, so the best possible round is the same for everyone and a tampered request cannot beat it. A naive per-frame random makes the board a lottery and the clamp a guess.

creative.title: A standing that cannot be farmed
creative.constraint: The board is public and the prize is real. If score were the sum of rounds, the winner would be whoever stood at the stand longest, and a player who could see the answers to trivia could simply wait out the clock.
creative.detail: Score is the best single round plus correct trivia points — never a sum of rounds. A question can be answered once, enforced by a unique key on (user, question) in the original and by a 409 here, and the correct index is never sent to the player: the trivia state endpoint strips it, and a timeout is submitted as `-1`. The result is a board where ten minutes of skill beats an hour of repetition, and the answer key never reaches the browser.

creative.title: A canvas that gives up its effects before it drops frames
creative.constraint: The game runs on whatever the visitor holds — a recent phone or a tablet from the stand's own shelf. A fixed visual budget that suits one device stutters on another, and a stutter during a sixty-second timed round costs real points.
creative.detail: The engine smooths a rolling frame time and, with hysteresis, drops its costly effects below about 38 fps and restores them only once frames are comfortably back above 50, so it does not flicker between modes. The pixel ratio is capped at 2 and each frame's time step is capped at 50 ms, so a tab that was in the background does not replay seconds of physics in one frame. Under reduced motion the timer ring becomes a plain number. A naive build either always runs flat or always runs rich and fails half the audience.

creative.title: A real Excel file, written without a library
creative.constraint: The lead list has to open in Excel, Numbers and LibreOffice, and in the demo it has to be built inside the tab with no server and no dependency to ship. An `.xlsx` is a ZIP of XML parts, and a participant list is exactly the kind of data that starts with `=` or `+`.
creative.detail: `xlsx.ts` is a dependency-free OOXML writer and `zip.ts` the container under it: STORED entries, a CRC-32 table built on first use, UTF-8 names. Cell values are typed by their JavaScript type, strings are XML-escaped and stripped of control characters, and text that begins with `= + - @` gets Excel's `quotePrefix` while no formula element is ever written, so a hostile company name cannot become a formula in the organiser's spreadsheet. Dates are real date serials read in Tbilisi time. The download is a genuine workbook, not a renamed CSV.

creative.title: Other visitors who play while you watch
creative.constraint: A live board with one player on it is a dead board, and a portfolio visitor has no crowd. The demo needs the standings to move without anyone clicking, and without inventing numbers that break the product's own rules.
creative.detail: Three seeded ghost players each play a round of the active event every 15 to 25 seconds, using demo-kit's seeded `createRandom` and `every`, which pauses while the tab is hidden and leaves no timer behind. A ghost's score never exceeds the event's budget and its catch breakdown adds up to the score exactly, so the drill-down in the console reconciles. Each round pushes a play and emits `play:created`, which invalidates the standings and Insights queries, so the board reorders with FLIP motion and the console numbers tick up. Fake activity that did not reconcile would be spotted the first time someone opened a player.

creative.title: A seed that is never out of date
creative.constraint: A fixture with absolute timestamps goes stale the day after it is written: the live event is over, nobody signed up recently and the thirty-day charts end last month. A demo that opens on an empty or closed event shows nothing.
creative.detail: The seed is authored as of one anchor instant, and `rebaseDates` shifts every field ending in `At` by the distance from that anchor to now, on load and on every reset. The live event is always from yesterday to tomorrow, the player's account always signed up two hours ago, and the charts always end today. Fair hours are written in UTC, so the hall day is 11:00 to 20:00 in Tbilisi wherever the visitor sits. It is the difference between a demo that works on the day it was built and one that works on any day.

creative.title: Errors that are keys, not sentences
creative.constraint: The interface is bilingual and the API speaks one language. A message string returned by a handler is in the wrong language for half its readers, and a form needs to know which input an error belongs to.
creative.detail: Handlers throw a `DemoApiError` that carries an i18n key and, for validation, a map of field to key. The UI renders `t(error.message)` and puts each field error under its own input. The same 760 keys exist in English and Georgian, and role guards (`requireUser`, `requireStaff`, `requireEditor`, `requireSuper`) refuse with keys too. A Georgian organiser never sees an English sentence leak out of a validator, and the wording lives with the translators rather than in the handlers.

highlights: Fair by construction: the round is planned up front so every player gets exactly the event's catchable budget and exactly its penalty budget on a four-stage ramp. Only the arrangement is random, and the server clamps a submitted score to the budget as well.

The standings rule is the best single round plus correct trivia points, never a sum of rounds, so time spent at the stand cannot buy a place on the board. The organiser can hide the board, and the player's card shows a countdown to the end instead of a rank.
Trivia is answered once and the correct answer is never sent to the browser. A timer auto-submits at zero, and the seconds-left counter turns red at five.
Four roles over one console: a supervisor reads, an admin edits events, items, trivia and prizes, a superadmin also manages people, and nobody can change, suspend or delete themselves.
Everything an organiser needs to run a fair day: schedule, round length, fairness caps, difficulty, speed level, board size and three visibility toggles per event.
The lead list leaves as a real Excel workbook, built so a hostile cell value cannot become a formula.
Georgian and English from the data model up: 760 strings in each language with the same keys, and Georgian-capable type throughout.
problem:
A stand at a trade fair is expensive and the conversation at it is short. Visitors drift past, glance at the banner and keep walking, and the ones who stop are asked to fill in a form with their name, company and number for no obvious reward. The organiser ends the day with a stack of cards, half of them illegible, and no way to say which sponsors actually held anyone's attention.

The organiser's side is no better: the schedule, the prizes, the questions and the list of who came live in different places, and the only fair way to pick a winner is one that nobody can argue with. A game fixes the first problem only if it is fair, because the moment a visitor suspects the score was luck or a trick, the prize and the lead are both worth less.
approach:
We made the game the reason to register and made fairness a property of the engine instead of a promise.

A visitor signs up, plays one sixty-second canvas round and is on the board. The round is planned before it starts, so every player faces the same total of catchable coins and the same total of penalties, arranged differently. Trivia adds bonus points on top, once per question, and the standing is the best round plus those points, so repetition does not help. The board refreshes while people watch.

Everything the organiser touches sits behind a console with four roles, so a staff member can look without being able to break anything. Events, falling items, trivia and prizes are all data the organiser edits, the people page handles accounts, and the participants page turns the lead list into an Excel file in one click. Sponsor items carry the brand names that make the game worth sponsoring.

architecture.detail: Next.js with the App Router and React 19. Server components fetch the data for the console and the standings; client components call a small set of `/api/*` route handlers for everything that mutates. Tailwind CSS 4 with Georgian-capable type and a monospace face for scores.

A custom HTML5 Canvas 2D engine with no game library: a pre-planned spawn schedule, a capped fixed-step loop, pointer, touch and arrow-key control for the paddle, and effects that drop on slow devices.
zod schemas on every route handler. The server clamps every submitted score to the event's point budget, and the round plan guarantees the same budget for every player.

Signed JWT sessions in an `httpOnly` cookie, passwordless sign-in with a one-time code, and a route gate that redirects signed-out visitors away from `/play`, `/me` and `/admin`. Four roles: player, supervisor, admin and superadmin.
A relational database through an ORM, with users, events, items, plays, trivia questions, answers and prizes. A unique constraint on (user, question) means a question can only be answered once.
Transactional mail for sign-in codes and for notifying prize winners, and object storage for the sponsor art an organiser uploads.
A server-built Excel workbook of the participant list, ready to import into a CRM.
Serverless, with the route handlers and pages deployed together. AI image generation for item art is planned: the button exists and answers coming soon.

results: A stand has a reason for people to stop and leave their details, and the organiser walks away with a clean lead list as an Excel file instead of a stack of cards.
Winners are decided by a rule nobody has to argue about: the same budget for every player, the best single round, and a server clamp behind it.
A whole event — its schedule, caps, items, trivia and prizes — is something an organiser edits in a console rather than something we deploy.
Staff can watch the standings, drill into a single player's plays and read the numbers on Insights without being able to change an event.
demoNote: A fictional re-skin of a real product we built, under the invented brand Tova, with every name, sponsor and person replaced. The Next.js server is gone: an in-browser mock answers all 41 API routes from seed data compiled into the bundle, so no network request is made. Data lives in memory and resets on reload, there is no real authentication, no email, no storage, and the Excel export is built in the tab. The demo opens signed out on the public landing page, and the demo bar signs you in as any of four roles.

name: Bani
tagline: One console for a company's whole voice estate — find any call on either phone platform, play its recording, check the backups, staff the agents and campaigns, and watch the platform's health, under per-role permissions.
summary: A voice operations console for a company whose telephony lives on two different phone platforms. It stitches the call records of both into single calls and rebuilds who transferred to whom, finds and plays the recording, backs recordings up and proves the backups are complete, staffs contact-centre agents and outbound campaigns, hands out phone extensions, and watches the health of the whole estate — with eight roles that each see only what they should. We built it end to end.
role: Full-stack. The call-record merge and transfer logic, the archive and verify jobs, the permission system, the contact-centre editors and the front end.

items: PostgreSQL (call-record import, self-test runs, locks, activity logs, settings)
MySQL (read access to the PBX database, mirrored)
LDAP directory bind and group mappings
Phone-platform and contact-centre admin APIs (REST, XML)
cron: record import, mirror interval, daily recording backup with a 7-day trailing retry, hourly self-test
In-process host collector (5 s samples, 60 s buckets, 30-day retention)

problem:
A company that runs its voice on two phone platforms ends up with two of everything. Two sets of call records, in different shapes, that describe the same afternoon differently. Two places recordings are kept, and a copy job nobody can prove has finished. A contact centre whose agents and campaigns are edited in a vendor tool built for one person at a time. And a list of who may touch each of those that lives in somebody's head.

The cost shows up as questions that should take a minute. Who did the customer actually speak to after the transfer? Is Tuesday morning's recording on the archive, or only on a box that has since been rebuilt? Which of the thirty agents staff the Georgian-language queue, and at what level? Each answer meant a different tool, a different login and a different person's permission.
approach:
The console puts one front on both platforms and keeps the rules in code that can be read.

Call records keep their own shapes underneath — one record per leg on the enterprise platform, legs linked by a shared id on the open-source PBX — and are brought together on read: legs are stitched into logical calls, and the party chain of every transfer is rebuilt from them. A search for a number is one search with one answer, and a call that bounced between three desks is one row you can open.

Recordings and their backups are treated as something to prove, not to hope for. A daily job copies recordings to a file archive with a trailing retry window, and a verify pass compares source and archive day by day, names what is missing on either side, and backfills the gap as a backup run of its own. Around that sit the contact-centre editors, the extension desk, the platform status page and the settings for every integration — and one permission table, with overrides an administrator can edit, that decides which of eight roles sees which of them.

architecture.detail: Next.js App Router. Server components check the feature before a page renders and redirect away from what a role may not open; client pages check again through a permissions endpoint, so a deep link cannot get around the navigation. Call access is also clamped per platform: a contact-centre role never sees the other platform's records.

Two sources read as one. The enterprise platform's call-detail files arrive over SFTP and are imported into PostgreSQL by a cron job (with reconcile and full-history modes); the open-source PBX's own database is mirrored on an interval and checked range by range. Merging legs into calls and rebuilding transfers is plain TypeScript.

Lookup, streaming and ZIP download from the voice-archive server. A daily cron with a seven-day trailing retry copies recordings to an SMB file archive; a verify pass compares both sides per day and backfills what is missing; an event log records every copy, skip and timeout.

The contact-centre platform's XML admin API, proxied by Next API routes and parsed in the client. The API changes one agent at a time, so writes are read-modify-write per agent and a bulk change reports failures per agent. A node monitor reads CPU, memory and uptime over SNMP.
A lock table with a 10-minute TTL, swept on read, merged with the PBX's own extension list. Reserve-then-create with a countdown on the page, and an audit trail with a purge.

An in-process collector samples the host every five seconds, writes 60-second buckets (average, minimum, maximum) kept for 30 days, and pings each configured backend. An hourly cron runs the self-test suite and stores every run in PostgreSQL.

Auth.js with a credentials provider and a JWT session carrying role and username. Directory users come from an LDAP bind with group-to-role mappings; local and API accounts sit beside them. One feature table with administrator overrides is enforced in the layout, the pages and the API.

The server, the databases, the directory, the file shares and SNMP are replaced by an in-browser mock API over seeded data, in a Vite SPA. The merge and transfer code is the same; the jobs are timers.

results: A search for a number answers across both platforms at once, and a transferred call is one row with its chain of parties instead of a pile of fragments.
A recording is a lookup, a player and a download — and "is it safely archived?" has an answer that is checked day by day instead of assumed.
Staffing a queue, changing a campaign and issuing an extension sit in one console with an audit trail, instead of in separate single-user vendor tools.
What each person can reach is a table an administrator edits and one function enforces, not an arrangement kept in someone's head.
The state of the whole voice estate — hosts, links, the self-test — is one page with history, so "was it like this yesterday?" has an answer.
demoNote: A fictional re-skin of a real product Boulder built: the company, the people, the numbers and the recordings are invented, and the product wears a new Georgian brand. There is no backend — an in-browser mock API answers every call, syncs, backups and self-tests are simulations on timers, and the three recordings are synthetic clips. Data lives in memory and resets on reload. Switch persona in the corner to see what each of the eight roles can reach.
